passage: At the city library in Stockholm, Astrid, two, heard a soft rattling from the music corner and toddled straight towards it. A boy was tipping a rain stick. She held out both hands. Her mother, Valentina, followed close. Astrid shook the stick, pressed her ear to it, then patted the bumpy rug and the cold glass of the fish tank. When she headed for the open staircase, Valentina scooped her up and carried her back to the rain stick.

qa.q: What sound did Astrid hear in the music corner?
qa.a: A soft rattling from a rain stick.

qa.q: What does Astrid moving towards every new sound and texture suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels curious and delighted by new things, drawn to explore without fear.

qa.q: What did Valentina do that kept Astrid's exploring safe?
qa.a: She followed close behind and scooped Astrid away from the open staircase, then brought her back to the rain stick.

qa.q: How might Valentina feel following Astrid around the library?
qa.a: She may feel amused and proud of Astrid's curiosity, but also watchful and alert to dangers.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving toward unfamiliar sounds and textures out of pure interest, with safety coming from the adult close by.

passage: The power went out on the hottest night of May, and the flat went dark. Avni, five, gasped. "Papa, we're in a cave! There are bats!" She hung a dupatta from the chair and crawled under it. "Why do bats sleep upside down? Do they get dizzy? Do bats eat roti?" Uday, her father, sweating by the torch, didn't say "Don't be silly." He handed her a roti and a banana. Avni rolled them together. "Cave pizza!" She fed a pretend bat first. When the fan whirred back to life, she groaned. "Can we keep the cave?"

qa.q: What did Avni roll together?
qa.a: A roti and a banana, calling it cave pizza.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the power went out?
qa.a: She felt excited and delighted, turning the dark flat into a cave full of bats.

qa.q: What did Uday do that gave Avni room to wonder?
qa.a: He didn't call her silly, answered her game by handing her food and let the make-believe continue despite the heat.

qa.q: How might Uday feel watching Avni feed a pretend bat?
qa.a: He may feel amused and fond of her imagination, even while hot and tired in the power cut.

grounding: Shows a child building a make-believe world, asking why questions and trying odd food combinations, excited by novelty and given room to wonder.

passage: In the village school near Hampi, Suraj, ten, had fallen for the old stone chariot. He knew how many wheels it had, which king built it, and he asked Nazia Madam impossible questions: "What if the river flowed backwards? Could they have built it without elephants?" But when she set ten rows of tables to copy, Suraj stared out of the window and wrote nothing. "It's pointless, Madam." Nazia Madam thought for a moment. "The chariot has four wheels. How many wheels for seven chariots? For twelve?" Suraj grabbed his pencil. By the end he had worked out the four-times table up to twenty chariots, and drawn every one.

qa.q: How many wheels does the chariot have, according to Nazia Madam?
qa.a: Four wheels.

qa.q: Why did Suraj stare out of the window instead of copying tables?
qa.a: He felt bored and unconvinced because copying rows felt pointless compared to the ideas he loved.

qa.q: How did Nazia Madam turn rote work into something Suraj enjoyed?
qa.a: She linked the tables to his passion by asking about chariot wheels, so the maths felt meaningful.

qa.q: How might Nazia Madam see Suraj's questions?
qa.a: She seems to see them as a sign of a lively, curious mind worth working with, not as a nuisance.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in a topic, enjoying hypotheticals and facts, resisting rote homework that feels pointless until it connects to his interest.

passage: Pranav, you asked why I wore black to Riya Didi's haldi last year. Honestly? I was fifteen and I wanted to reject everything. I'm Jyoti, and that year I listened only to heavy metal, read philosophy books I half understood, and told Dadaji over dinner that rituals were superstition. I loved arguing. I'd argue for God one night and against God the next, just to see where the idea went. It felt electric, like my brain was growing. But at the haldi, everyone was laughing and dancing, and I sat in a corner in black, proving a point nobody cared about. That's when I realised saying no to everything wasn't the same as thinking for myself. Now I choose. I still argue with Dadaji. But I sang at Diwali, because I wanted to.

qa.q: What colour did Jyoti wear to the haldi?
qa.a: Black.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when arguing both sides of big questions?
qa.a: Jyoti felt electric and alive, as if the mind was growing.

qa.q: What did Jyoti learn at the haldi?
qa.a: That rejecting everything was not the same as independent thinking, so Jyoti now chooses what to keep, like singing at Diwali.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt about the dinner-table arguments?
qa.a: Dadaji may have felt challenged and perhaps hurt at first, but also engaged, since they still argue now.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning customs and trying new music and philosophies, enjoying arguing both sides, and realising rejecting tradition isn't the same as independence.

passage: Last Karva Chauth, my daughter Mehak, sixteen, put down her spoon and asked her mother, "Why do only women fast for their husbands? Why doesn't Papa fast for you?" I'm Yogesh, her father, and I felt the room tilt. My first urge was to say, "Because that's how it is." My chest felt tight; I worried she was throwing away everything we'd taught her. But I also felt a strange pride. It was a sharp question. So I didn't answer straight away. I asked, "What makes you ask?" She talked for twenty minutes about fairness. I listened. At the end I said, "I don't have a perfect answer. Maybe I'll fast next year too." She laughed. Now she brings her questions to me first.

qa.q: On which occasion did Mehak ask her question?
qa.a: On Karva Chauth, at dinner.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when Mehak asked why only women fast?
qa.a: He felt unsettled and anxious, his chest tight, but also proud of her sharp question.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that kept the door open?
qa.a: He listened first by asking what made her ask, heard her out for twenty minutes and admitted he didn't have a perfect answer.

qa.q: How might Mehak see her father now?
qa.a: Mehak seems to see him as someone safe to question, since she now brings her questions to him first.

grounding: Shows a parent unsettled when his teenager questions a long-held custom, feeling both anxiety and pride, and choosing to listen first.

passage: The trip to the hill station had already changed plans three times, and now dense fog had cancelled the morning train. The group chat exploded: "Let's just take any bus!" "Or a shared cab?" "Or go somewhere else?" Swati, twenty, felt her stomach knot. She liked knowing where she'd sleep and what she'd eat. Pallavi, who loved surprises, teased her: "Relax, it's an adventure." But Swati had already done what she always did. She'd printed the state bus timings the night before and saved the hotel's number. "There's a bus at eleven from the main depot. I've checked the seats." The chat went quiet. Then Pallavi wrote, "Okay, Swati's plan." By evening they were eating momos in the hills, exactly on time.

qa.q: What cancelled the morning train?
qa.a: Dense fog.

qa.q: How did Swati feel as the plans kept changing?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and anxious, her stomach knotting because she likes knowing what comes next.

qa.q: What strength did Swati's steady style bring the group?
qa.a: Her reliable preparation, printed bus timings and saved hotel number, gave the group a workable plan.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Swati after the trip?
qa.a: Pallavi may see her steady style as dependable rather than boring, since Swati's plan got them there on time.

grounding: Shows a young adult who prefers clear plans and feels uneasy with constant changes, and whose steady style brings reliability despite a cancelled train.

passage: I play bass in our college band, so I've watched this up close. I'm Siddharth. Last month, Farhan wanted to play only old ghazals, exactly as recorded. Neha wanted to remix everything with electronic beats. They'd started calling each other "boring uncle" and "attention seeker." Lakshmi, our singer, didn't pick a side. I don't know what she was thinking, but I saw what she did. She asked Farhan, "What does keeping the old songs pure protect for you?" He said his late grandfather sang them. Then she asked Neha what the remixes meant to her. Neha said she wanted younger people to hear them. Lakshmi said, "So you both want the songs to live." They agreed on one pure ghazal and one remix. The labels stopped.

qa.q: What instrument does Siddharth play?
qa.a: Bass.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel watching Lakshmi handle the argument?
qa.a: Siddharth seemed impressed and relieved, noticing how she calmed things without taking sides.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that respected both styles?
qa.a: She asked each person what their preference protected, found their shared goal and avoided labelling either as dull or shallow.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Lakshmi asked about the old songs?
qa.a: He may have felt respected and understood, able to share that his late grandfather sang them.

grounding: An observer describes a young adult who respects both traditional and very open styles, asking what each protects and avoiding labels.

subtype: Observer of a very open peer [Observer]
passage: In the Barcelona design office, Omar, twenty-five, sat next to Ines. In one year she had started a podcast, learned to sail, moved flats twice and pitched eleven new product ideas. Some colleagues rolled their eyes. "Ines and her next big thing." Omar found her exciting to work beside; her ideas were often the freshest in the room. But he'd also noticed that most of them faded after a week. One Friday she showed him three new sketches. Omar said, "These are brilliant. Which one would you want to see finished by June?" Ines paused. "The recycling app." "Then let's break it into steps." They wrote a plan on the whiteboard. Three months later, the app had its first test users.

qa.q: How many new product ideas had Ines pitched in a year?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How does Omar feel about working beside Ines?
qa.a: He finds it exciting and admires her fresh ideas, though he also notices they often fade.

qa.q: How did Omar help Ines turn ideas into follow-through?
qa.a: He asked her to choose one idea to finish by June and helped break it into steps on the whiteboard.

qa.q: How might Ines feel when her app gets its first test users?
qa.a: Ines may feel proud and satisfied, seeing one of her many ideas finally completed.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a very open peer who keeps switching interests, seeing richness where others see flakiness, and helping her follow through.

passage: At Nani's house on Eid, guests kept arriving, and the pile of shoes by the door grew into a mountain. Hafsa, five, frowned at it. She sat down and lined up every pair, big to small, toes to the wall. When her cousins knocked over her half-built block tower and ran off, she stamped her foot and cried, "It's not finished!" Her Khala, Nazia, helped her rebuild it. Later Nazia said loudly to everyone, "Who made the shoes so neat?" Hafsa pointed at herself, grinning. All evening she stayed calm, checking the row whenever the bell rang.

qa.q: What did Hafsa line up at Nani's house?
qa.a: Every pair of shoes, big to small, toes to the wall.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when her cousins knocked over the tower?
qa.a: She felt upset and frustrated, stamping her foot because the game was left unfinished.

qa.q: What did Nazia do that helped Hafsa?
qa.a: She helped rebuild the tower and praised the neat shoes in front of everyone, which made Hafsa proud.

qa.q: How might the guests feel finding their shoes lined up?
qa.a: They may feel amused and pleased, surprised that a five-year-old kept the doorway so tidy.

grounding: Shows a child who lines up shoes, gets upset at an unfinished game and feels calmer and proud when her tidying is noticed, despite a crowded Eid gathering.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Aparna, ten, packed her school bag every night before dinner: books in timetable order, pencils sharpened, water bottle filled. On Saraswati Puja week, while the colony children rehearsed their dance, she stayed home to finish her homework first. When she crossed out one word in her essay, she tore out the page and started again, worried it looked messy. Her teacher, Manjula Ma'am, made her class monitor because she never forgot anything. But at break one day, Manjula noticed Aparna sitting inside, revising again. "Aparna, the monitor gets a break too. Go and play for ten minutes." Aparna hesitated, then ran out. She came back pink-cheeked and laughing.

qa.q: What did Aparna pack every night before dinner?
qa.a: Her school bag: books in timetable order, pencils sharpened, water bottle filled.

qa.q: Why did Aparna tear out the essay page?
qa.a: She felt worried and uneasy that one crossed-out word made it look messy.

qa.q: What did Manjula Ma'am do that was wise?
qa.a: She trusted Aparna's reliability as monitor but also noticed her missing play and sent her out for a break.

qa.q: How might Manjula Ma'am see Aparna?
qa.a: She sees her as reliable and trustworthy, but also as a child who needs rest and play.

grounding: Shows a diligent child who packs her bag early, finishes homework first and worries about small mistakes, trusted by her teacher though play gets squeezed out.
